content_list.content_text: The leader of the change was François Truffaut (1932-1984), writing for Cahiers du Cinéma, a magazine launched in April 1951 by critics André Bazin, Jacques Doniol-Valcroze and Joseph-Marie Lo Duca. Truffaut read the first issues of Cahiers in military prison in early 1952. By the following year, he was already writing for the magazine. In 1954, he contributed a call to the barricades. "A Certain Tendency of the French Cinema" was a polemical article against what he despised, which he called le cinéma de papa.

information.contentText: Simone Signoret and Anton Walbrook in La Ronde. The play the film was based on, Reigen, inspired David Hare's play The Blue Room.

content_list.content_text: The young critic attacked filmmakers who had specialized in tasteful literary adaptations. There was more to his revolt than mere contempt for the conservative style he saw embodied in the work of Jean Aurenche (1903-1992) and Pierre Bost (1901-1995), the leading screenwriters of the period, and of directors such as Claude Autant-Lara (1901-2000) and Yves Allégret (1907-1987). "Several producers of the time had collaborated with the Germans during the war," filmmaker Marcel Ophüls (b. 1927) added regarding Truffaut's essay. "So there were many reasons to try to get rid of that oppressive influence and, at the same time, to root out the unions' stranglehold on French cinema."

Truffaut extolled American B movies at the expense of the impassive, self-styled French cinema "of quality". He passionately championed a more personal style of directing, in which filmmakers could take risks and leave a unique stamp on their work. This was the birth of what became known as "la politique des auteurs". By the end of the 1950s, however, French cinema had produced several films that belied the decade's image as complacent and superficial.

information.contentTitle: Scene from The Wages of Fear (1953)
information.contentText: Some of the opening scenes set in the town were cut because they reflected the political climate of the time.

content_list.content_text: Le Salaire de la peur (The Wages of Fear, 1953), by Henri-Georges Clouzot (1907-1977), about truck drivers hauling nitroglycerin along the potholed roads of South America, is a frenetic action film that keeps the viewer riveted. His Les Diaboliques (Diabolique, 1955) is a superbly frightening thriller with a plot full of twists. Beyond these, La Ronde (1950) by Max Ophüls, an adaptation of Schnitzler set in Vienna (but shot in France), is a stylized, sophisticated and caustic account of the love lives of a group of interconnected characters. In fact, French cinema of the 1950s was much more interesting and complex than Truffaut's article suggests. It was not a decade in which a group of young cinephiles simply watched the films of Alfred Hitchcock and Howard Hawks (1896-1977) at the Cinémathèque, scorning the previous generation and then launching their own careers as directors.

information.contentText: With murder on her mind, Véra Clouzot plays Christina in Diabolique. Psycho author Robert Bloch said this was his favorite horror film.

content_list.content_text: Established filmmakers such as Henri-Georges Clouzot (1907-1977), Robert Bresson (1901-1999), Georges Franju (1912-1987), Jacques Becker (1906-1960), Jacques Tati (1907-1982), René Clément (1913-1996), Max Ophüls (1902-1957), René Clair (1898-1981) and Jean Renoir (1894-1979) made important films during what proved to be a transitional decade in the history of the French film industry. Long before Truffaut, and by the end of the decade, Jean-Luc Godard (b. 1930) and his Cahiers colleagues had begun shooting their own films. Other filmmakers were also already clashing with the previous generation.

content_list.title: Truck Drivers on Film
content_list.description:
With its endless combination of wheels, landscape and machismo, the world of truck drivers has served as the backdrop for melodramas such as They Drive by Night (1940), by Raoul Walsh (1887-1980), and Thieves' Highway (1949), by Jules Dassin (1911-2008). The international success of The Wages of Fear gave rise to variations with more exotic settings: the Sahara in Ice Cold in Alex (1958) and the Ivory Coast in The Big Gamble (1961).

The intimidating size of trucks inspired not only raucous comedies in the 1970s, among them Smokey and the Bandit (1977) and Convoy (1978), but also the remarkable debut film of Steven Spielberg (b. 1946), Duel (1971), which draws on the simplicity of its premise: Dennis Weaver believes a truck driver wants to kill him. In Roadgames (1981), by Richard Franklin (1948-2007), genial trucker Stacy Keach realizes he has attracted the attention of a maniac.

content_list.content_text: Agnès Varda's (b. 1928) debut film, La pointe courte (1955 - which she describes as a bombshell of nonconformity), was released in 1955. Drawing on Brecht and William Faulkner's modernist novel The Wild Palms, the 25-year-old director told two parallel stories. La pointe courte was not a box office success, but it showed a young filmmaker far removed from the "tradition of quality" that Truffaut so despised.

It is also debatable whether the prolific and versatile Aurenche and Bost were really as conventional as Truffaut claimed. "Truffaut shot at the wrong target (...) He should have attacked the directors, not the screenwriters," Bertrand Tavernier later wrote in defense of the pair. "By attacking Aurenche, he attacked the person closest to the New Wave - the person who was already ready to experiment and who was the most open." Tavernier hired Aurenche as a screenwriter on several of his films in the 1970s, among them L'horloger de St Paul (The Watchmaker of St. Paul, 1974).

quote.quote: If anyone needs convincing of the joys and rewards of minimalism in cinema, A Man Escaped is the best place to start.
quote.author: Critic Adrian Martin on A Man Escaped

content_list.content_text: French cinema of the 1950s was characterized, in a way, by its great technical masters, such as René Clément. His film Jeux interdits (Forbidden Games, 1952), about two children who use fantasy to cope with trauma and death during World War II, was attacked by some as sentimental, but it won the Golden Lion in Venice and the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film.

information.contentText: French Resistance fighter Fontaine in A Man Escaped. The film is based on the true story of André Devigny during the war.

content_list.content_text: Clément had worked with Jean Cocteau (1889-1963) on La belle et la bête (Beauty and the Beast, 1946) and directed a fine film about the Resistance, La bataille du rail (The Battle of the Rails, 1946), but he had the misfortune of being labeled a conservative filmmaker. Claude Autant-Lara suffered the same fate. Among his best-known films of the decade are the caustic comedy L'Auberge Rouge (The Red Inn, 1951) and an adaptation of Stendhal's Le Rouge et le Noir (1954). Damaging as Truffaut was to his reputation, it was nothing compared to the disgrace Autant-Lara brought upon himself late in life by getting involved in right-wing politics and supporting the Nationalist Party.

After leaving Hollywood and returning to Europe, Max Ophuls revisited thoroughly French themes in a series of period films made in the 1950s. Le plaisir (1952) was adapted from three stories by Guy de Maupassant. The atmosphere of Madame de... (The Earrings of Madame de..., 1953), set in turn-of-the-century Paris and revolving around a story of lost earrings and infidelity, is summed up by the moment when a man realizes his marriage is "only superficially superficial". The settings may be the boudoirs and ballrooms of high society, but the characters' suffering was all too real.

information.contentText: Many films highlight the absurdities and cruelties of life by portraying them through the eyes of children, yet few have done so more effectively and poignantly than René Clément's masterpiece, Forbidden Games. Clément draws extraordinarily expressive and convincing performances from his young leads, free of mawkishness; there is an instinctive grace in the boy's kindness toward his little friend. Narciso Yepes contributes a lyrical solo guitar score, expressive in its simplicity.

content_list.content_text: After almost 15 years away, Jean Renoir returned to his homeland to make French Cancan (1954), set in belle époque Montmartre. His best film was Casque d'Or (1952), an intensely romantic evocation of the Parisian underworld of the 1890s. Almost its equal was the crime film Touchez pas au grisbi (1954), which revived the acting career of Jean Gabin.

That film had a great influence on postwar French crime cinema - as can be seen in the minimalism of Du rififi chez les hommes (Rififi, 1955), by Jules Dassin (1911-2008), shot on location, with an exuberantly laconic narrative style and a celebrated silent safecracking sequence that lasts almost half an hour. A similarly somber atmosphere pervades Bob le flambeur (1956), by Jean-Pierre Melville (1917-1973), about an aging gangster who plans to rob a casino. The French approach to film noir displayed a melancholy lyricism that would later influence American films of the genre.

information.contentText: Casque d'Or was coldly received on its release in France, but it later came to be admired by future leading lights of the French New Wave for the way it evokes the past with (in François Truffaut's words) "tenderness and violence".

content_list.content_text: Robert Bresson, another director attacked by the Cahiers group, created an existentialist masterpiece with Un condamné à mort s'est échappé (A Man Escaped, 1956), about a French Resistance fighter imprisoned by the Nazis who spends his time planning his escape. Truffaut admired its spare style. As he himself wrote, this was "one of those films of which one can say that it does not contain a single useless shot, nor one that could have been cut or shortened. It is the very opposite of films that look like a montage, a collage of images". As his words attest, French cinema of the 1950s was not as stagnant as he himself suggested in his famous essay for Cahiers.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the text by Geoffrey Macnab, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp.

movies.title: Casque d'Or
movies.overview: Ex-convict Georges Manda returns to the free world determined to go straight and takes a steady job as a carpenter. Unable to completely shake his connections with the underground, he meets with a former prison mate, older gangster Félix Leca, who introduces him to his mistress, the sweet but guarded Marie "Casque d'Or". Marie and Georges fall into a passionate relationship, driving Félix to do everything in his power to ruin the couple.

movies.title: The Wages of Fear
movies.overview: In the South American jungle, supplies of nitroglycerine are needed at a remote oil field. The oil company pays four men to deliver the supplies in two trucks. A tense rivalry develops between the two sets of drivers on the rough remote roads where the slightest jolt can result in death.

movies.title: Forbidden Games
movies.overview: Orphaned after a Nazi air raid, Paulette, a young Parisian girl, runs into Michel, an older peasant boy, and the two quickly become close. Together, they try to make sense of the chaotic and crumbling world around them, attempting to cope with death as they create a burial ground for Paulette's deceased pet dog. Eventually, however, Paulette's stay with Michel's family is threatened by the harsh realities of wartime.

movies.title: Diary of a Country Priest
movies.overview: An inexperienced, sickly priest shows up in the rural French community of Ambricourt, where he joins the community's clergy. But the locals don't take kindly to the priest, and his ascetic ways and unsociable demeanor make him an outcast. During Bible studies at the nearby girls school, he is continually mocked by his students. Then his attempt to intervene in a family feud backfires into a scandal. His failures, compounded with his declining health, begin to erode his faith.

movies.title: Rififi
movies.overview: Out of prison after a five-year stretch, jewel thief Tony turns down a quick job his friend Jo offers him, until he discovers that his old girlfriend Mado has become the lover of local gangster Pierre Grutter during Tony's absence. Expanding a minor smash-and-grab into a full-scale jewel heist, Tony and his crew appear to get away clean, but their actions after the job is completed threaten the lives of everyone involved.

movies.title: Hiroshima Mon Amour
movies.overview: The deep conversation between a Japanese architect and a French actress forms the basis of this celebrated French film, considered one of the vanguard productions of the French New Wave. Set in Hiroshima after the end of World War II, the couple -- lovers turned friends -- recount, over many hours, previous romances and life experiences. The two intertwine their stories about the past with pondering the devastation wrought by the atomic bomb dropped on the city.

content_list.title: Timeline of Events from 1940 to 1959
content_list.description: Asian cinema gains even more prominence with the release of several masterpieces. Film noir emerges and musicals continue to shine on the big screen. The Western holds on to its reign as one of the most popular genres, and one of the most important movements in cinema takes place in France: the French New Wave.
